entries.meaning: Weakened by affection for Raghubara, the company covered two leagues as the sun declined. They found water and ground, camped through the night, and at dawn set out from love for Raghunātha. Meanwhile, near the night’s end, Rāma awoke because Sītā had seen a dream: Bharata seemed to have arrived with the whole company, his body scorched by separation from his lord; all the mothers appeared pale, anguished, and unlike themselves. Hearing the dream, Rāma’s eyes filled with tears and even the remover of anxiety fell under anxiety’s power. Lakṣmaṇa said the dream was not good and might announce severe bad news. Then the brothers bathed, worshiped Śiva, and honored the holy people.

Sītā’s lord again became absorbed in worry: why was Bharata coming? Someone arrived and reported that he was accompanied by no small fourfold army. Hearing this, Rāma was deeply concerned—on one side stood his father’s word, on the other his reserve before his brother. Understanding Bharata’s nature in his heart, the Lord could find no settled ground for anxiety; at last he found reassurance in knowing Bharata to be wise and holy. Lakṣmaṇa perceived the burden in Rāma’s heart and, considering policy suited to the moment, said: ‘Lord, without being asked I say something; a servant who is never boldly insistent at the needed time is no true servant. You are the omniscient crest-jewel of masters; I speak as your follower according to my understanding. You know everyone’s love and trust from your own thoroughly simple, loving heart, treasury of affection.’

Lakṣmaṇa argued: ‘When a sense-bound creature gains authority, delusion makes his nature visible. Bharata is devoted to right policy and is a discerning saint; the whole world knows his love for your feet. Yet today, upon gaining the royal position, even he may have crossed the bounds of duty. Seeing a crooked relation and a bad opportunity—Rāma alone in exile—he may have formed evil counsel, assembled his forces, and come to make the kingdom undisputed. Imagining a million crooked plans, both brothers may have gathered troops. If there were no deceit in the heart, why would chariots, horses, and elephants seem fitting? Who can blame Bharata alone? The world goes mad on obtaining sovereignty. The moon approached his guru’s wife; Nahuṣa mounted brahmins; and wicked Vena turned from world and Veda—royal intoxication corrupted them.’

‘Sahasrabāhu, Indra, and Triśaṅku—whom has royal pride not stained? Bharata has chosen the proper method: leave no enemy or debt even in the smallest remainder. But he failed in one respect by despising Rāma as helpless; he will understand that especially today when he beholds Rāma’s angry face in battle.’ As Lakṣmaṇa spoke, the savor of policy gave way to the savor of combat, and the tree of martial ardor flowered through the guise of gooseflesh. Bowing at the Lord’s feet and placing their dust upon his head, the naturally strong speaker of truth said: ‘Do not judge my words improper, Lord. Bharata has treated us with no small contempt. How long must we endure and suppress the mind, when you are beside me and a bow is in my hands? I am born a Kṣatriya in Raghu’s line, Rāma’s follower as the world knows; dust kicked even with a foot rises onto the head of a contemptible man.’

Lakṣmaṇa rose, joined his hands, and asked permission, as though the heroic spirit had awakened from sleep. Binding his matted hair, tightening the quiver at his waist, and readying bow and arrow, he declared: ‘Today I shall win honor as Rāma’s servant and teach Bharata a lesson in battle. He and his brother will receive the fruit of dishonoring Rāma and sleep upon the battlefield. The whole company has arrived at a fortunate time; today I shall openly release my long-held anger. As a lion crushes a herd of elephants and a hawk snatches and enfolds a quail, so I shall strike down Bharata with his army and younger brother. Even if Śiva comes to his aid, I shall defeat him in battle, invoking Rāma.’ Seeing Lakṣmaṇa inflamed with great wrath and hearing his authoritative oath, every world grew afraid and its guardians wanted to flee in panic.

The world sank in fear, and a voice arose in the sky praising Lakṣmaṇa’s immense strength: ‘Dear one, who can describe or know your glory and power? Whatever the deed, fitting or unfitting, everyone says it should be performed after reflection. Those who act rashly and later regret are not wise, say the Vedas and learned people.’ Hearing the divine words, Lakṣmaṇa felt ashamed; Rāma and Sītā honored them. Rāma said: ‘Dear brother, your political judgment is sound; the intoxication of kingship is hardest of all. Only kings who have served no assembly of saints grow drunk without even tasting it. But hear me, Lakṣmaṇa: no one like Bharata has been heard of or seen in Brahmā’s creation. Royal pride could not touch him even if he gained the offices of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Can droplets of sour gruel ever destroy the ocean of milk?’

Rāma continued: ‘Young darkness might swallow the young sun, the sky might dissolve into a cloud, Agastya might drown in a cow’s hoofprint, earth might forsake her natural forbearance, or a gnat’s breath might blow Mount Meru away—but royal pride could never enter Bharata. By my oath and our father’s, Lakṣmaṇa, no pure and excellent brother equals him. Merit is milk and fault is water; the Creator mixes them to fashion the world. Bharata is the swan born upon the lake of the Solar line: he separated virtue from fault, took the milk of goodness, left the water of defect, and made his own fame brighten the world.’ Speaking of Bharata’s virtues, character, and nature, Raghurāya submerged in the ocean of love. Hearing his words and seeing his affection for Bharata, the gods praised him: who else is such a compassionate Lord?

The gods said: ‘Had Bharata not been born in the world, who would have borne the whole weight of duty upon earth? His virtues are inaccessible to poets; who but you, Raghunātha, truly knows them?’ Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā rejoiced to hear the celestial voice. Meanwhile Bharata, with all his companions, bathed in the sacred Mandākinī. Leaving the people near the river and obtaining the mothers’, guru’s, and ministers’ permission, he set out with Śatrughna and Guha toward Sītā and Raghurāya. Remembering his mother’s deed, he felt ashamed and imagined millions of fears: ‘May Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā not hear my name, rise, abandon this place, and go elsewhere. Even if they count me party to my mother’s counsel, whatever they do will be little; may they forgive my sins and faults and receive me from their own gracious side.’

Bharata thought: ‘If they reject me as foul-minded, or honor me as a servant, Rāma’s sandal is still my refuge. Rāma is a perfect master, though every servant has faults. Like the cātaka and fish, vessels of fame in the world, I am newly skilled only in my own vow and love.’ Thinking thus he proceeded, every limb weakened by mingled reserve and affection. At one moment his mother’s wrong seemed to turn him back; the next, the strength of devotion and the axle of courage carried him forward. When he remembered Raghunātha’s nature, his feet hurried upon the path. Bharata’s state was like an insect caught within a current, sometimes carried one way and sometimes another. Seeing his anxiety and affection, even the Niṣāda became bodiless with absorption. Reading favorable signs, Guha said Bharata’s grief would vanish and joy arise—though sorrow would return in the outcome.

Knowing Guha’s words true, Bharata approached the hermitage. He saw the community of forest and mountain like a delighted hungry person finding good food. His state resembled subjects distressed by calamity, fear, the three afflictions, and hostile planets who reach a happy country under good rule. The wealth of the forest where Rāma dwelt shone like contented subjects under a noble king. Detachment was the minister, discernment the king, and the charming sacred forest the realm; self-restraint and observances were warriors and the mountain the capital; peace and good understanding were the pure, lovely queen. Every limb of that good kingdom was complete, with its heart joyfully resting at Rāma’s feet. King Discernment, with his army, had defeated the ruler Delusion and now governed the city unhindered amid happiness, prosperity, and favorable times.
